content.p: In the first week of March 1906, United States Army troops climbed an extinct volcano on Jolo Island in the southern Philippines and attacked the people sheltering in its crater. The American press and officers first called it the First Battle of Bud Dajo. Critics in the United States later called it a slaughter, Mark Twain among them, and writers and senators have since argued over whether the word "battle" fits what happened on the mountain. The number of dead is still disputed. Estimates of the Moro dead run from about 600 to more than 1,200, and the American dead were between 15 and 21 soldiers, depending on the source.

The event matters for two reasons. It shows how the United States ran its rule over Muslim communities in Mindanao and Sulu, and it shows how an official account can shape what the public later believes. The record is thin partly because the government released little. The story below draws on the historian Kim A. Wagner's study of the case, on contemporary newspapers as quoted in later accounts, and on Philippine commentary in the century since.

The United States took over the Philippines from Spain in 1898, and the war against Filipino forces in the north ran until 1902. The Moro peoples of Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago had a separate history. HistoryNet, drawing on the account of the period, says the Moros had occupied their homelands for some 500 years and had not joined the Filipino insurrection. They expected the Americans to leave the Sulu territory in their hands.

That did not happen. After negotiations at Zamboanga, Brigadier General J. C. Bates reached an agreement with Sultan Amir and 19 datus. Under it the Moros recognized American sovereignty over foreign affairs and law enforcement, while the sultan and datus kept most internal affairs. HistoryNet notes that the agreement covered only the Sulu Islands. When talks with the sultanate of Mindanao failed, the first of many armed clashes between Moro communities and the Americans followed. HistoryNet links the crisis at Bud Dajo to an earlier death: in 1905 a man named Pala, wanted for murder by British authorities in north Borneo, was killed with several of his cohorts and a U.S. soldier when he resisted troopers who tried to arrest him at the Tambang Pass. HistoryNet says his death "only raised tensions."

Foreign Affairs, reviewing Wagner's book, describes Moro families who had left their villages on Jolo after the American takeover and resettled around the crater of Bud Dajo. Wagner's own account, quoted by Prospect, is that the Moros' decision to fortify the hill was "an act of desperation to defend their faith and community" against American authorities who were encroaching on their traditions and way of life.

Bud Dajo is a volcano of about 2,000 feet, with hundreds of families living around its crater. Foreign Affairs, reviewing the book, reports that Major General Leonard Wood, a Harvard-educated former army surgeon who governed the Moro Province, had ordered his forces to "capture and destroy" the encampments on the mountain. Wood had made the subjugation of the Moro Province a personal matter, according to Foreign Affairs. American commanders, the same review says, told their soldiers to shoot on sight. Hugh L. Scott, district governor of Jolo, was on leave in the United States when he wrote his June 1906 annual report. In it he said the Moros who fled to the crater "declared they had no intention of fighting, ran up there only in fright, and had some crops planted and desired to cultivate them" (Prospect, quoting Scott).

Philstar, in a 2010 column, gives the sequence of dates as 5 March, when the bombardment of the crater began, to 7 March, when the fighting ended. It quotes Wood's own view of the Moros as "nothing more than nor less than an unimportant collection of pirates and highwaymen", and says he intended that the Moros would either submit or suffer harsh consequences. Philstar also reports that more than 600 American troops were sent to deal with the problem. Pimentel, the Philippine senator, gave a different figure of 800 American troops in his 2006 speech. The sources here also differ on the troop numbers and the casualties.

The Moros had few modern weapons. The Senate's record of Pimentel's speech, citing the book Swish of the Kris by Vic Hurley, describes the defenders as armed only with krises, spears and a few rifles. Foreign Affairs says they fought with obsolete cannons, old rifles, spears, knives and gunpowder in shells.

Most accounts here describe many of the dead as women and children, although Wood's letter, quoted below, says the women were armed and charged with the men. Foreign Affairs quotes Captain Edward Lawton, who led a column of the 19th Infantry up the eastern side. Lawton wrote that "the whole crest of the mountain was covered with corpses." He described bodies with "wounds of every description" and of "little helpless babies, some with a number of wounds, groping amid the mass of dead for the mother's breast."

Prospect, reviewing Wagner's book, says American units killed more than 1,200 Moro men, women and children at Bud Dajo. It reports that troops fired machine guns at women and children who had already surrendered, and that many of the wounded were killed where they lay. It compares the toll with the dead at My Lai and Wounded Knee. Literary Review, reviewing the same book, gives a lower figure of "an estimated one thousand" dead after a three-day fight. Foreign Affairs writes that Wagner describes a massacre of up to 1,000 men, women and children. The Senate's 2006 tribute gives about 1,000 Moro dead, and says that only six of the defenders escaped.

The figure SunStar attributes to President Rodrigo Duterte in 2016 is lower. In remarks to a Reuters reporter on 5 September 2016, Duterte referred to the killing of 600 Moro people in 1906. SunStar reports that he said the United States had not even apologized for its atrocities in that period. The gap between 600 and more than 1,200 is not explained by any single source; each figure is the estimate of the person or book that gave it.

American casualties were also reported differently. Philstar gives 15 killed and about 32 wounded. Literary Review gives 18 killed and fifty-nine wounded. Pimentel's 2006 speech and Prospect's account of Wagner's book give 21 killed, with 75 and 73 wounded respectively.

Philstar quotes a cable from President Theodore Roosevelt to Wood, which congratulated him and his officers and men on "the brilliant feat of arms wherein you and they so well upheld the honor of the American flag." The New York Times headline that Philstar quotes read "WOMEN AND CHILDREN KILLED IN MORO BATTLE. PRESIDENT WIRES CONGRATULATIONS TO TROOPS."

The cable did not settle the matter. Prospect says the events were debated in the Senate and the House later that March, with Democrats criticising the Republican administration. Literary Review says Democrat politicians called on the government for an official explanation. Prospect reports that the government released only a handful of telegrams already in the public domain, and never published the evidence that would have allowed a fuller assessment. Some newspapers suggested a deliberate cover-up. Literary Review says the story was "quickly buried" until a single photograph survived. Prospect says detailed information emerged in the summer of 1906 through unofficial channels, as officers and correspondents on leave began returning from the Philippines.

Wood defended the operation in his letters. Prospect quotes a letter from Wood to the Secretary of War, William Howard Taft, in which he wrote that "Moro women wore trousers and were dressed, armed much like the men, and charged with them," and that children "were in many cases used by the men as shields." Prospect says Wood used this to justify the killings by stressing the victims' savagery.

Some commentary backed the army. Prospect quotes a Harper's Weekly editorial that offered the "victors at Dajo Hill" its "respectful and sympathetic thanks for having completed what seems to have been a warrantable job of extermination." Mark Twain, by contrast, wrote that the massacre "was no brilliant feat of arms" and that the troops had "dishonored" the flag. Prospect says Twain kept his full account for an autobiography published only after his death in 1910.

Much of the public record of Bud Dajo rests on a photograph. Literary Review says a former soldier, Aeronaut Gibbs, took a picture of the aftermath showing exhausted American soldiers posing beside a trench full of bodies, "like hunters after a successful shoot." Moorfield Storey, president of the Anti-Imperialist League, sent a copy to W. E. B. Du Bois in 1907. Du Bois wanted to distribute an enlarged version to show what he saw as the injustice of American rule in the Philippines.

In the Philippines the event entered local memory in a different form. Foreign Affairs says Bud Dajo remains deeply etched in Moro memory and is passed down through kissa, traditional epic songs. Philstar notes that the Moros' resistance at the crater came to be remembered as the Moro Crater Massacre. In 2006 Senator Pimentel said that "by no stretch of imagination" could Bud Dajo be termed a battle, because the defenders were armed with krises, spears and a few rifles against a modern force. He argued that the Moros had broken the law, but that the American response had been a slaughter.

In 2016 President Rodrigo Duterte cited the killings and said the United States had not even apologized for its atrocities of that period. Wagner's book is a detailed study of the case. Foreign Affairs says Wagner argues that the killings were not an aberration, and that Bud Dajo set a pattern in which abuse was followed by a cursory inquiry, a cover-up, impunity and erasure.

The main questions about Bud Dajo have no settled answer. The first is the number of dead on the mountain. Figures from 600 to more than 1,200 appear in print, and the basis for each is not always given. Prospect and Foreign Affairs both use Wagner's research, but give different ranges. The second is the number of troops, which is given as more than 600 by Philstar and 800 by the Senate's record. The third is the number of women and children among the dead. Wagner and Prospect describe large numbers; Wood's own letter presented the women as armed combatants. The official record that could settle these points was largely not released.

The historian Wagner's book, and the reviews of it, make clear that the sources disagree. Where a figure appears here it is attributed to the person or publication that gave it, and the record should be read with that in mind.
